extracted.intended_audience: Comedians, comedy industry professionals, scholars, journalists, and general readers interested in comedy ethics and intellectual-property issues
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, evaluating, and responding to instances where a performer uses another person's comic material without credit; covers definitions, community norms, legal recourse, defenses, and examples across stand-up, TV, and other media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of joke theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke theft is the act of performing and taking credit for comic material written or performed by another person without their consent and without acknowledging the other person's authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is framed as potentially a form of plagiarism and, in some cases, copyright infringement. Use this definition as the baseline test: did Person A perform material originated by Person B and fail to seek consent or provide acknowledgement? Examples in the article (various accused comics) illustrate real-world disputes; ambiguity can remain when origin is unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with plagiarism and copyright infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke theft may be a form of plagiarism and can, in some cases, be copyright infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal liability depends on copyright law and proving authorship/derivation; historically there has been very little legal recourse, though some lawsuits have resulted in financial compensation (e.g., Jay Mohr/Rick Shapiro dispute). The page notes 'There is, historically, very little legal recourse taken in cases of joke theft.' Consider both civil remedies and practical difficulties proving origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Hack' label and community stigma
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic known to steal jokes may be labelled with the epithet 'hack'; a 'hack comic' uses material that is unoriginal or which is blatantly copied from its original author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community labeling and reputation damage are primary social sanctions. Practitioners evaluate whether material is 'original' or 'blatantly copied' and may ostracize or mock suspected thieves. Historical and contemporary accusations (e.g., Carlos Mencia, etc.) show reputational consequences often outweigh legal ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity from simultaneous/coincidental discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cases of alleged joke theft are ambiguous, due to the possibility of simultaneous and coincidental discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites a sociological study noting 'most instances of possible joke theft are ambiguous, owing to the potential for simultaneous and coincidental discovery.' When assessing theft, consider independent creation, shared cultural tropes, and the likelihood of prior exposure. Anti-pattern: assuming theft solely from similarity without provenance evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses: satire, calque, borrowing, and inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics sometimes defend re-use of others' jokes as satire, as a calque (word-for-word translation), or as 'borrowing' or taking inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the reuse transforms, parodies, or translates material (which may weigh against theft), or merely copies it. The article gives examples where performers claim such defenses; treat claims of satire/calque/borrowing as factors but not definitive exoneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vaudeville-era etiquette: 'add to the joke and make it his own'
rubrics_metrics.description: In music halls and vaudeville, etiquette only required that 'the borrower add to the joke and make it his own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, borrowing with modification was acceptable practice. When measuring modern ethical standards, consider whether the alleged borrower substantially adapted or added original material, versus verbatim copying. Historical norms differ from contemporary expectations and legal frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-media effect on perceived ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: The first comic to tell a stolen joke on some sort of media became the one associated with the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media exposure (albums, television, cable, internet) can establish public association regardless of origin. When assessing claims, note timing of appearances and recordings: being first on a widely distributed medium often fixes public attribution and increases perceived ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized recordings as a facilitator of theft
rubrics_metrics.description: The widespread use of video camera-equipped smartphones led to an increase in unauthorized recordings of live comedy shows, which may have facilitated joke theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comics often request no unauthorized audio/video recordings to reduce the risk of their material being copied and spread. When advising performers, recommend clear venue policies and enforcement to limit unauthorized capture and sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited legal recourse and practical enforcement difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: There is historically very little legal recourse taken in cases of joke theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although copyright law can apply, practical obstacles—proving originality, tracking dissemination, and costs—limit litigation. The page documents that some suits occurred and some were financially compensated, but overall legal enforcement is rare; many disputes are handled informally within the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-enforced consequences (ban, confrontation, violence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics have chosen to exact their own justice; examples include physical altercations, bans from venues, and other informal punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions can include venue bans (e.g., Joe Rogan banned from The Comedy Store after a confrontation), confrontations, and reputational retaliation. These consequences arise from peer enforcement rather than formal institutions; they signal the community's role in policing originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persona or act theft beyond individual jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations can extend beyond single jokes to claims that a comic stole another performer's persona, act, or attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should consider holistic similarities in persona, delivery, and stage persona, not only textual overlap. The Denis Leary/Bill Hicks case is cited where peers alleged theft of act and persona; such claims affect broader judgments of authenticity and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap inevitability and finite joke-space argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Some defenders argue there are only a finite number of jokes, making overlap inevitable; this is used to explain apparent similarities across shows and media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging alleged theft, weigh the plausibility of independent convergence given common themes and limited joke constructions. The article cites defenses from creators who argue homage or inevitable overlap; such arguments reduce the probative force of surface similarity without provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-media appropriation and attribution errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes in film and television are often taken from comics or other media, and journalists or shows sometimes incorrectly attribute jokes to the wrong performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate provenance across media (columns, TV, stand-up recordings). Attribution errors by third parties complicate ownership claims. Examples (Cavett, Woody Allen, The Naked Gun/Get Smart) illustrate how material migrates and how false attribution can mislead assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern detection and public exposure mechanisms (social media, blogs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online accounts and social media (e.g., CopyComic, blogs, Facebook/Twitter/YouTube) have been used to expose alleged plagiarism and to compile examples of similar material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public exposés can shape community consensus quickly and bring attention to alleged theft. When evaluating such sources, verify comparisons and context; social media can amplify accusations but may also oversimplify or misattribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological interpretation: accusations reflect community perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations of joke theft can reflect peers' perceptions of a suspicious comic's membership in the stand-up community and overall craft as much as the similarity between jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes, consider the social dynamics: newcomers, outsiders, or perceived low-craft comics may be more readily accused. Use sociological insight to temper judgments based solely on textual similarity and to account for power, status, and network effects in accusation dynamics.
